primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: Severe systemic illness alters thyroid hormone metabolism at multiple levels. A common early pattern is reduced peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion from decreased type 1 deiodinase activity and altered tissue uptake, with reduced clearance of reverse T3; cytokine and hypothalamic-pituitary effects can further lower TSH and T4 as illness becomes more severe or prolonged.
vignette: A 67-year-old man with no history of thyroid disease is in the intensive care unit with severe bacterial pneumonia and septic shock. On hospital day 4, thyroid tests obtained because of persistent fatigue show low serum T3, a free T4 concentration within the reference range, and a TSH concentration in the low-normal range. Reverse T3 is elevated. There is no goiter, thyroid tenderness, or prior thyroid medication use.
lead: Which change most directly contributes to this patient’s thyroid hormone pattern?
correct: Reduced peripheral type 1 deiodinase activity, decreasing conversion of T4 to T3 and clearance of reverse T3
distractors: Stimulation of thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins at the TSH receptor, increasing thyroid hormone synthesis
Destruction of thyroid follicles with release of preformed T4 and T3 into the circulation
Loss of thyroid hormone receptor beta function in the pituitary, impairing negative feedback
Increased thyroxine-binding globulin synthesis, increasing total thyroid hormone while preserving free hormone
distractor_notes: TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies cause Graves hyperthyroidism with increased T4/T3 and suppressed TSH, not the low-T3 pattern of severe nonthyroidal illness.
Destructive thyroiditis causes transient release of stored thyroid hormone and a thyrotoxic biochemical pattern rather than isolated low T3 with elevated reverse T3.
Thyroid hormone receptor beta resistance causes elevated free T4/T3 with inappropriately nonsuppressed TSH, the opposite of this critical-illness pattern.
Increased TBG changes total hormone concentrations but generally does not produce this low free/total T3 illness pattern with elevated reverse T3.
key_expl: This is nonthyroidal illness syndrome. In severe illness, peripheral thyroid hormone metabolism changes before there is necessarily any intrinsic thyroid-gland disease. Decreased hepatic and peripheral type 1 deiodinase activity reduces conversion of T4 to active T3 and also reduces deiodination/clearance of reverse T3, producing low T3 with increased reverse T3. With more severe or prolonged illness, altered hypothalamic-pituitary signaling, cytokines, binding proteins, transport, and other deiodinases can further lower TSH and T4. The syndrome should therefore not be reduced to a single universal laboratory pattern.
objective: Recognize the low-T3 pattern of nonthyroidal illness as a consequence of altered peripheral thyroid-hormone metabolism, especially reduced T4-to-T3 conversion and impaired reverse-T3 clearance.
clues: severe systemic illness without prior thyroid disease
normal free T4 early in the illness

sources.support: Endotext describes low T3 as the earliest/common biochemical change during starvation and severe systemic illness and explains that multiple alterations of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis and peripheral metabolism contribute.

sources.organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf
sources.title: Metabolism of Thyroid Hormone — Endotext
sources.support: Endotext states that nonthyroidal illness often produces decreased plasma T3 and increased reverse T3 through diminished hepatic D1-mediated T4-to-T3 conversion and impaired reverse-T3 deiodination, with additional contributions from transport and D3.
